title: Bug: rsyslog service takes long time to restart at boot in Debian 13 causing test which depend on syslog to fail
author: tirupatihemanth
body:
### Is it platform specific

generic

### Importance or Severity

Critical

### Description of the bug

At the startup of sonic we have rsyslog-config.service which restarts the rsyslog.service. During this restart the amount it takes to stop the rsyslog service increased from ~1sec to ~4seconds in Debian 13. 

```
root@sonic:/var/log# journalctl -u rsyslog
Feb 06 01:52:38 sonic systemd[1]: Stopping rsyslog.service - System Logging Service...
Feb 06 01:52:42 sonic systemd[1]: rsyslog.service: Deactivated successfully.
Feb 06 01:52:42 sonic systemd[1]: Stopped rsyslog.service - System Logging Service.
Feb 06 01:52:42 sonic systemd[1]: Starting rsyslog.service - System Logging Service...
Feb 06 01:52:43 sonic systemd[1]: Started rsyslog.service - System Logging Service.
```

This delay in rsyslog restart is causing some tests which depend on syslog at startup to fail. For instance consider the test: test_fast_reboot https://github.com/sonic-net/sonic-mgmt/blob/8f460cb453c315e1a3d7e68e2aae6436ae9dcd7b/tests/platform_tests/test_advanced_reboot.py#L88

It fails with error because the test checks for the presence of LAG_READY messages in syslog for each portchannel present. When teamd emits these messages if the rsyslog service is down we don't see all of these messages causing the test to fail

```
Failed: Advanced-reboot failure. Failed test: test_fast_reboot[sonic], failure summary:
[('test_fast_reboot[sonic]None', ['FAIL: Event LAG_READY was found 5 times, when expected exactly 8 times'])]
```

Here are the lag messages immediately after rsyslog restart but we missed three out of 8 portchannels 
```
syslog:2844:2026 Feb  6 01:52:43.229801 sonic NOTICE teamd#tlm_teamd: :- try_add_lag: The LAG 'PortChannel104' has been added.
syslog:2855:2026 Feb  6 01:52:43.289550 sonic NOTICE teamd#tlm_teamd: :- try_add_lag: The LAG 'PortChannel105' has been added.
syslog:2881:2026 Feb  6 01:52:43.353699 sonic NOTICE teamd#tlm_teamd: :- try_add_lag: The LAG 'PortChannel106' has been added.
syslog:2895:2026 Feb  6 01:52:43.395552 sonic NOTICE teamd#tlm_teamd: :- try_add_lag: The LAG 'PortChannel107' has been added.
syslog:2919:2026 Feb  6 01:52:43.460182 sonic NOTICE teamd#tlm_teamd: :- try_add_lag: The LAG 'PortChannel108' has been added.

```

whereas on Debian 12 we see

```
Feb 06 02:26:58 sonic systemd[1]: Stopping rsyslog.service - System Logging Service...
Feb 06 02:26:59 sonic systemd[1]: rsyslog.service: Deactivated successfully.
Feb 06 02:26:59 sonic systemd[1]: Stopped rsyslog.service - System Logging Service.
Feb 06 02:26:59 sonic systemd[1]: Starting rsyslog.service - System Logging Service...
Feb 06 02:26:59 sonic systemd[1]: Started rsyslog.service - System Logging Service.
```

Systemd security sandboxing directives are the root cause of the slow rsyslog shutdown on Debian 13. rsyslog unit file in Debian 13 has the following additional directives present by default

```
NoNewPrivileges=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
PrivateDevices=yes
ProtectHome=yes
ProtectSystem=full
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectClock=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
ProtectHostname=yes
```

Once these features were disabled with an override unitfile the amount of time it takes for rsyslog service to stop becomes less than a second and we were able to receive all the LAG messages.

```
# /etc/systemd/system/rsyslog.service.d/override.conf
[Service]
PrivateTmp=no
PrivateDevices=no
ProtectHome=no
ProtectSystem=no
ProtectKernelTunables=no
ProtectKernelModules=no
ProtectClock=no
ProtectControlGroups=no
ProtectHostname=no
```
This test shouldn't depend on syslog to detect portchannels are up, it should find an alternate way. Community must make a decision here.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Restart the switch
2. After startup check: journcalctl -u rsyslog 
3. Check for "try_add_lag" messages (example shown above) saying PortChannel is added. (Reproduction should be on a switch with PortChannels)
4. No. of try_add_lag messages must match No. of PortChannels on the system. But we miss some of them. 

### Actual Behavior and Expected Behavior

Expected behaviour is the test to pass

linkedPullRequests.title: [rsyslog] Fix Trixie restart delay with conditional restart
linkedPullRequests.author: rustiqly
linkedPullRequests.body:
#### Why I did it
On Debian 13 (Trixie), `rsyslog.service` includes systemd sandboxing directives (`PrivateTmp`, `ProtectSystem`, `ProtectKernelTunables`, etc.) that add ~4 seconds of overhead per restart due to namespace setup/teardown. This causes syslog-dependent tests to fail by missing log messages during the extended restart window.

Fixes #25382

#### How I did it
Instead of always restarting rsyslog after generating the config, we now:

1. Generate the config to a unique temp file (`mktemp`)
2. Compare with the existing `/etc/rsyslog.conf` using `cmp -s`
3. **Config changed** (or first boot): install the new config and restart rsyslog
4. **Config unchanged**: send `SIGHUP` to rsyslog to re-open log files without a full restart

The `SIGHUP` fallback is critical — it ensures rsyslog re-opens its file handles even when the config has not changed (needed after log rotation or `/var/log` remounts), while completely avoiding the 4-second namespace teardown/setup cycle. This preserves the upstream Trixie sandboxing directives.

Additional hardening:
- `mktemp` for unique temp files with `trap`-based cleanup on exit
- Explicit first-boot handling (missing `/etc/rsyslog.conf`)
- Error handling on `cp` failure (do not restart with stale config)

#### How to verify it
1. Build a VS image with this change
2. Boot and verify rsyslog is running: `systemctl status rsyslog`
3. Run `config reload` — rsyslog should NOT restart (config unchanged), only SIGHUP:
   ```
   journalctl -u rsyslog --since "1 min ago"
   # Should show rsyslog re-opening files, NOT a stop/start cycle
   ```
4. Change a syslog config (e.g., add a remote server), run `config reload` — rsyslog should do a full restart
5. Run `syslog/test_logrotate.py` — both test cases should pass (SIGHUP re-opens files after /var/log remount)

No. From the man page:

```
HUP
    This lets rsyslogd perform close all open files.
```

comments.author: tirupatihemanth
comments.body:
@rustiqly  rsyslogd v8.2504.0 doesn't support reload and HUP behavior isn't implemented to reload the config. 

We don't want to remove the sandboxing features and also we don't want the 4 second delay on every restart/warm-restart/fast-restart because rsyslog configuration doesn't change on every reboot. I suggest an alternate way:

We can add a check in rsyslog-config.sh script to restart the rsyslog service only when there is a change in the rsyslog.conf file that was currently loaded into rsyslog service.  We accept the delay in the cases where we actually change the configuration (or on first boot). Changing rsyslog configuration often is not a frequent use case AFAIK. This approach should fix all the sonic-mgmt errors we currently see on various restart/warm-restart tests. Something like this:

```
sonic-cfggen -d -t /usr/share/sonic/templates/rsyslog.conf.j2 \
    -a "{\"udp_server_ip\": \"$udp_server_ip\", \"hostname\": \"$hostname\", \"docker0_ip\": \"$docker0_ip\", \"forward_with_osversion\": \"$syslog_with_osversion\", \"os_version\": \"$os_version\", \"syslog_counter\": \"$syslog_counter\"}" \
    > /tmp/rsyslog.conf.new

if ! cmp -s /tmp/rsyslog.conf.new /etc/rsyslog.conf; then
    cp /tmp/rsyslog.conf.new /etc/rsyslog.conf
    systemctl restart rsyslog
fi
rm -f /tmp/rsyslog.conf.new
```

@saiarcot895  do you agree?

comments.author: rustiqly
comments.body:
Thanks @tirupatihemanth and @saiarcot895 — you're absolutely right that SIGHUP doesn't reload rsyslog config. Reworked the approach completely:

**Before:** Attempted `reload-or-restart` with SIGHUP (doesn't work)
**After:** Conditional restart — generate config to temp file, compare with current, only restart when config changed.

```bash
sonic-cfggen ... > /tmp/rsyslog.conf.new
if ! cmp -s /tmp/rsyslog.conf.new /etc/rsyslog.conf; then
    cp /tmp/rsyslog.conf.new /etc/rsyslog.conf
    systemctl restart rsyslog
fi
rm -f /tmp/rsyslog.conf.new
```

This avoids the ~4s Trixie sandboxing delay on reboot/warm-restart/fast-restart where rsyslog config is unchanged. Removed the systemd ExecReload override entirely.

Updated PR title and description to match.

```
=== Test: config unchanged → no restart ===
SKIP (config unchanged) ✅

=== Test: no existing config (first boot) → restart ===
```

Three cases tested:

2. **Config changed** (syslog server modified) → restart as before ✅
3. **First boot** (no existing config) → restart to apply initial config ✅

VS VM is currently offline so couldn't test end-to-end, but the `cmp -s` logic handles all edge cases correctly.

linkedPullRequests.title: [rsyslog]: Use RELP instead of UDP for forwarding from container to host
linkedPullRequests.author: saiarcot895
linkedPullRequests.body:
<!--
     Please make sure you've read and understood our contributing guidelines:
     https://github.com/Azure/SONiC/blob/gh-pages/CONTRIBUTING.md

     ** Make sure all your commits include a signature generated with `git commit -s` **

     If this is a bug fix, make sure your description includes "fixes #xxxx", or
     "closes #xxxx" or "resolves #xxxx"

     Please provide the following information:
-->

#### Why I did it

When the host's rsyslog is restarted (for example, to regenerate the config after some changes, or as part of some automated script), there is a chance that some syslog messages from the containers are lost. Most of the time, this isn't an issue. However, if there are test cases that expect all syslogs to be present (such as the advanced-reboot test case), then this can cause a problem. Additionally, this could affect debuggability of issues where a rsyslog restart happens in the middle.

There are two options for reliable message transport in rsyslog: TCP and RELP. With TCP, while the protocol knows whether a syslog message has been delivered or not, the application doesn't know, because there is no feedback from the remote side saying the message was received. This means that there is still a chance that messages could be lost when the connection is broken (if, for example, the host rsyslog gets restarted), because after the connection is established, the sender rsyslog (in the container) doesn't know if the message has been received or not.

RELP builds on top of TCP, and adds a feedback mechanism where the remote side notifies the sender whether the message has actually been received or not. This makes it much less likely to lose a message. There is one known possible case where a message (or messages) could be lost: the network is down, and rsyslog gets restarted. This at least requires both the network and rsyslog to have an issue, rather than just one. There is also a slim possibility where a message could get duplicated; this should be mostly fine (hopefully).

RELP does require that both sides are using a recent version of rsyslogd (at least 7.3.16, which looks like it was released more than 10 years ago), but since we use Debian on both the container and the host, it should be fine.

Therefore, switch to using RELP when sending syslog messages from the container to the host. Also, enable a linked list queue on the sending queues on both the container rsyslog and on the host rsyslog. This means that if the sending of a log message fails (either because there is no network/route to the destination, or, thanks to RELP, messages are not getting acknowledged as received), it will be queued in that linked list and retried later.

Additionally, since messages that were generated in the past could now be delivered later, change the timestamp that is recorded into `/var/log/syslog` to be the timestamp that the log message was generated (i.e. sent from the original application) rather than the log message was received by this rsyslogd instance. This more accurately reflects when an event happened, and with queueing and RELP now involved, the difference could be on the scale of seconds. This does mean that messages in `/var/log/syslog` may appear out-of-order at times.

#### User-facing behavior changes

This PR will change the timestamp that is recorded into `/var/log/syslog` to be the timestamp that the syslog message was generated, rather than when the syslog message was received by rsyslogd on the host. This means that some messages in `/var/log/syslog` may appear out-of-order. For example,

```
2026 Mar 31 02:46:05.498008 vlab-01 NOTICE swss#orchagent: :- doTask: Removed pending neighbor DEL operation for PortChannel101:fc00::72 after SET operation
2026 Mar 31 02:46:05.594737 vlab-01 NOTICE swss#orchagent: :- flushFdbEntries: flush key: SAI_OBJECT_TYPE_FDB_FLUSH:oid:0x21000000000000, fields: 1
2026 Mar 31 02:46:05.594760 vlab-01 NOTICE swss#orchagent: :- recordFlushFdbEntries: flush key: SAI_OBJECT_TYPE_FDB_FLUSH:oid:0x21000000000000, fields: 1
2026 Mar 31 02:46:05.185039 vlab-01 NOTICE syncd#syncd: message repeated 20 times: [ :- get: get switch attr: SAI_SWITCH_ATTR_FDB_AGING_TIME]
2026 Mar 31 02:46:05.596281 vlab-01 NOTICE syncd#syncd: :- flushFdbEntries: generating fdb flush notifications
2026 Mar 31 02:46:05.596312 vlab-01 NOTICE syncd#syncd: :- flushFdbEntries: flushing 24 dynamic entries
2026 Mar 31 02:46:05.596323 vlab-01 NOTICE syncd#syncd: :- meta_sai_on_fdb_flush_event_consolidated: processing consolidated fdb flush event of type: SAI_FDB_ENTRY_TYPE_DYNAMIC
2026 Mar 31 02:46:05.598454 vlab-01 NOTICE syncd#syncd: :- meta_sai_on_fdb_flush_event_consolidated: fdb flush took 0.002123 sec
```

The syslog message at `02:46:05.185039` was processed and logged after the message at `02:46:05.594760` (although in this particular case, I suppose there's a chance that rsyslogd held the "message repeated x times" message until it had the final count and then sent it, and the message generated timestamp could be from when the first instance of that message was logged).

Here is a more egregious case:

```
2026 Mar 31 02:44:45.160717 vlab-01 DEBUG unix_chkpwd: nss_tacplus: user_priv[13] { gid=0, info=NULL, group=NULL, shell=NULL }
2026 Mar 31 02:44:45.160750 vlab-01 DEBUG unix_chkpwd: nss_tacplus: user_priv[14] { gid=0, info=NULL, group=NULL, shell=NULL }
2026 Mar 31 02:44:45.160811 vlab-01 DEBUG unix_chkpwd: nss_tacplus: user_priv[15] { gid=1000, info=remote_user_su, group=sudo,docker, shell=/bin/bash }
2026 Mar 31 02:44:32.725033 vlab-01 NOTICE swss#orchagent: :- start: Performing SaiRedis log rotate
2026 Mar 31 02:44:45.160420 vlab-01 NOTICE swss#orchagent: :- addNextHopGroup: Create next hop group 10.0.0.59@PortChannel102,10.0.0.61@PortChannel103,10.0.0.63@PortChannel104
2026 Mar 31 02:44:45.372153 vlab-01 INFO python3.13[191789]: ansible-ansible.legacy.command Invoked with _raw_params=vtysh -c "show ip route 192.223.168.0/25 json" _uses_shell=True expand_argument_vars=True stdin_add_newline=True strip_empty_ends=True argv=None chdir=None executable=None creates=None removes=None stdin=None
2026 Mar 31 02:44:45.687503 vlab-01 DEBUG sudo: nss_tacplus: server[0] { addr=10.250.0.102:49, key=t*****, timeout=5 }
```

The log rotate message was processed 13 seconds after it was initially generated. I'm not sure why there's so much of a delay in this case.

Fixes #17792
Fixes #25382
May help with sonic-net/sonic-mgmt#11311

##### Work item tracking
- Microsoft ADO **(number only)**: 28314311

#### How I did it

Modify the `rsyslog.conf` file on the host and the container to use RELP instead of UDP.

In addition, update the syntax used for the config files to the (newer) RainierScript format, which, among other things, makes it easier to set settings for specific outputs.

Also, enable retries for messages that failed to be forwarded, retrying for up to 60 times before dropping the message.

Finally, modify `rsyslog.conf` to write the timestamp that the log message was generated, not when it was received. This makes it a bit easier to correlate events, at the cost of making the logs look out of order.
